Lower Bounds The sample complexity bounds we prove in Theorem 1, 3, and 5 are optimal (up to log factors) in terms of the dependence on d, n, and log(1/δ). However, the question remains of resolving the optimal dependence on the bag size k. For every function class F, we have the trivial lower bound on the minimax sample  complexity of n = Ω(d log(1/δ)/(kε)) for the realizable setting and n = Ω d log(1/δ)/(kε2 ) for the agnostic setting, since LLP with n bags is only harder than supervised learning with nk examples. In general, the 1/k dependence in the lower bound cannot be improved, as there are function classes for which it is tight. For example, consider the function class F = {f0 , f1 } where fi (x) = i for i ∈ {0, 1}. For this class F, observing the label proportion α allows us to compute the average instance-level classification loss over the bag for both f0 and f1 . Therefore, LLP with n bags is no harder than supervised learning with nk labeled examples, so F can be PAC learned with O(1/(kε)) e samples 2 in the realizable setting and O(1/(kε )) in the agnostic setting. e

However, to the best of our knowledge, Theorem 1 is the first result which provides a concrete generalization bound for bounded VC classes for the EPRM learning rule. A few comments about Theorem 1 are in order. • The assumption that F is symmetric is mild and due to technical reasons. Note that any nonsymmetric F can be enlarged to a symmetric one with VC dimension at most 2d + 1. • The bag size assumption is technically required, and we conjecture it can be removed. It is a mild assumption since if one has bags of size k ≤ 10, then one can preprocess the dataset to combine sets of bags to form a larger bag of size at least 11, and then compute fbEPRM on the preprocessed dataset. This achieves the same guarantee (albeit with smaller range of ε).

First, we show via standard uniform convergence arguments that the predictor fbEPRM must have small population proportional matching error. Next, we relate the proportion matching error to the classification error to show that fbEPRM must have classification error L(fbEPRM ) ∈ / [ε, 1 − ε]. Finally, we show that fbEPRM must have classification error L(fEPRM ) ≤ ε, as otherwise we would have selected the predictor 1 − fbEPRM . b Step 1.
